overview: On the command line, every program can read text coming in, write text going out, and report errors separately. Pipes, redirection, and chaining are the three simple mechanisms that let you connect these text flows together like sections of plumbing.

A pipe (the | symbol) takes the output of one command and feeds it straight into the next command as its input, so you can build a little assembly line where each tool does one small job. Redirection sends output into a file (or reads input from a file) instead of the screen, using symbols like >, >>, and <. Chaining operators (;, &&, ||) let you run several commands in a row and control what happens based on success or failure.

In data engineering these three ideas are everywhere: you search a giant log for errors, sort and count them, save a filtered slice of a CSV to a new file, quietly discard noise, and run a download step followed by a processing step only if the download worked. Learning them turns a pile of separate tools into a single readable one-line pipeline.
learningObjectives: Explain the three standard streams (standard input, standard output, and standard error, numbered 0, 1, and 2) and how commands read from and write to them.
Use the pipe | to feed one command's output into another, and use redirection (>, >>, <, 2>, 2>&1, &>, /dev/null) to move output to and from files.
Chain commands with ;, &&, and || to run steps sequentially or conditionally, and combine pipes, redirection, and chaining into real data-engineering pipelines.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Pipes, redirection, and chaining are shell features that connect and sequence the standard streams of processes. Every process is given three streams: standard input (stdin, file descriptor 0), standard output (stdout, file descriptor 1), and standard error (stderr, file descriptor 2). A pipe (|) connects the stdout of one process to the stdin of the next, creating a pipeline of concurrently running processes. Redirection operators attach a stream to a file instead of the terminal: > and >> send stdout to a file (overwrite or append), < reads stdin from a file, 2> redirects stderr, 2>&1 duplicates stderr onto stdout's destination, and &> sends both to a file. Chaining operators sequence commands: ; runs them one after another unconditionally, && runs the next only if the previous exited with status 0 (success), and || runs the next only if the previous exited non-zero (failure).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of each command as a small machine with an in-tray, an out-tray, and a separate complaints box. Normally the out-tray and complaints box both dump onto your screen. A pipe (|) is a conveyor belt that carries one machine's out-tray straight into the next machine's in-tray, so you can line up machines to do a job in stages. Redirection is telling a machine to drop its out-tray into a labelled folder (a file) instead of onto the screen - > empties the folder first, >> adds to the end. Chaining is a to-do list: ; means 'do this, then that'; && means 'do that only if the first one worked'; || means 'do that only if the first one failed'. That is the whole idea.
coreConcept.historicalContext: The pipe was introduced into Unix in 1973 by Doug McIlroy, whose insight became a founding principle of the Unix philosophy: write small programs that do one thing well and connect them through text streams. Ken Thompson added the | operator to the shell, and almost overnight it changed how people worked - instead of one giant program, you composed many tiny ones. Redirection of standard streams to and from files predates it slightly and comes from the same design, where 'everything is a file', including your keyboard, screen, and the special discard device /dev/null. The conditional operators && and || arrived with later shells like the Bourne shell and Bash to make scripting robust. Decades later this composable, text-stream model is exactly why the command line remains the backbone of data engineering.

whyItMatters.business: Being able to search, filter, and count inside massive data and log files in seconds - without loading them into any application - lets teams answer urgent questions ('how many failed orders today?') immediately, keeping decisions and dashboards moving.
whyItMatters.engineering: Pipes let engineers assemble a custom data tool on the spot from small building blocks, and redirection captures results to files that later steps or scripts can consume, turning ad-hoc investigation into reusable automation.
whyItMatters.scalability: A pipeline streams data through one record at a time, so the same one-line command that summarizes a small file also works on a file too large to open in an editor, and can be dropped unchanged into a script that runs across thousands of files.
whyItMatters.cost: Doing quick filtering and summarizing with lightweight command-line tools avoids spinning up heavier systems or clusters for simple questions, saving both compute cost and engineer time.
whyItMatters.reliability: Chaining with && ensures a processing step only runs when the previous step truly succeeded, and separating standard error from standard output means real errors are never silently mixed into your results - both are essential for trustworthy pipelines.

coreComponents.name: Standard streams (stdin, stdout, stderr)
coreComponents.definition: The three text channels every command is given: standard input (fd 0) for data coming in, standard output (fd 1) for normal results, and standard error (fd 2) for error and diagnostic messages.
coreComponents.purpose: To give programs a consistent way to receive input and to separate their normal results from their error messages so each can be handled independently.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Deliver input to the program, carry its normal output somewhere (screen, file, or next command), and keep error messages on a distinct channel so they can be shown, saved, or discarded separately.
coreComponents.examples: stdin (0) = keyboard or piped data | stdout (1) = normal results | stderr (2) = warnings and errors

coreComponents.name: The pipe operator (|)
coreComponents.definition: A symbol placed between two commands that connects the first command's standard output directly to the second command's standard input.
coreComponents.purpose: To pass data from one tool to the next without a temporary file, so several small commands form one processing pipeline.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Run the connected commands at the same time, stream text from the left command's stdout into the right command's stdin, and let each stage do its single job on the flowing data.
coreComponents.examples: grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

coreComponents.name: Redirection operators (>, >>, <, 2>, 2>&1, &>)
coreComponents.definition: Symbols that reattach a command's streams to files instead of the terminal - sending output into a file, appending to it, reading input from a file, or steering error output.
coreComponents.purpose: To save results for later, feed a file into a command, and control where normal output versus error output goes.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Create or open the target file, write or append stdout to it, supply stdin from a file, and redirect or merge stderr as instructed - all before the command's normal work begins.
coreComponents.examples: > file (overwrite) | >> file (append) | < file (input) | 2> errors.log | 2>&1 | &> all.log | 2>/dev/null (discard errors)

coreComponents.name: Chaining operators (;, &&, ||)
coreComponents.definition: Symbols placed between whole commands that decide whether and when the next command runs, based on order and on the previous command's exit status.
coreComponents.purpose: To run a sequence of steps and control the flow so later steps only happen when it makes sense (for example, only after a successful download).
coreComponents.responsibilities: Run commands in order (;), run the next only on success (&&), or run the next only on failure (||), using each command's exit code (0 = success) to decide.
coreComponents.examples: step1 ; step2 (always) | download && process (only if download worked) | test -f data.csv || echo 'missing'

internalWorking: When the shell sees a pipeline like 'grep ERROR app.log | sort', it creates a pipe - a small in-memory buffer with a read end and a write end - then starts both commands at roughly the same time as separate processes.

It connects the write end of the pipe to grep's standard output (fd 1) and the read end to sort's standard input (fd 0). Now anything grep prints as normal output flows into sort instead of the screen; grep's standard error still goes to the terminal.

The commands run concurrently and stream data: as grep finds matching lines it writes them into the pipe, and sort reads them as they arrive. If sort is slow, the pipe buffer fills and grep automatically pauses until there is room - this back-pressure keeps memory bounded even for huge inputs.

For redirection like '> out.txt', the shell opens (or creates and truncates) the file before the command runs and points that command's stdout at the file's descriptor instead of the terminal; '>>' opens the file in append mode so existing content is kept. '2>' does the same for the error stream, and '2>&1' makes fd 2 point to wherever fd 1 currently points.

For chaining, the shell runs each command, reads its exit status when it finishes, and applies the operator: ';' just moves on, '&&' proceeds only if the status was 0, and '||' proceeds only if the status was non-zero - so the exit code is the hidden signal that controls the whole flow.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Data source (file or keyboard) -> command 1 reads stdin & writes stdout -> pipe | carries stdout to next stdin -> command 2 filters/transforms -> pipe | -> command N summarizes -> redirection > or >> writes final stdout to a file -> stderr (2) flows separately to screen, a log, or /dev/null -> shell reads exit codes and chaining (&& / ||) decides the next step
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An engineer wants to know which error types are most common in a 2 GB log file, so they start with 'grep ERROR app.log', which reads the file and prints only the lines containing ERROR to its standard output.
2. A pipe sends those lines into 'sort', which arranges identical lines next to each other; sort reads the stream from the pipe as its standard input rather than from the keyboard.
3. Another pipe feeds the sorted lines into 'uniq -c', which collapses runs of identical lines into one line each, prefixed by a count of how many times it appeared.

4. A final pipe sends those counted lines into 'sort -nr' to order them by count highest-first, and the finished summary either prints to the screen or is redirected with '> error_summary.txt' to save it for a report.

keyTerminology.term: Standard input / output / error (stdin, stdout, stderr; fd 0, 1, 2)
keyTerminology.meaning: The three numbered text streams every process gets: 0 is where it reads input, 1 is where it writes normal output, and 2 is where it writes error and diagnostic messages.
keyTerminology.importance: Knowing that normal output (1) and errors (2) are separate channels is what lets you save results cleanly while logging or discarding errors independently.

keyTerminology.meaning: A connector that routes the standard output of the command on its left into the standard input of the command on its right, with the two commands running at the same time.
keyTerminology.importance: The pipe is the single most powerful command-line idea: it lets you build a custom data pipeline from small tools without ever creating a temporary file.

keyTerminology.meaning: The exit status is a number a command returns when it finishes (0 = success, non-zero = failure); /dev/null is a special 'black hole' file that discards anything written to it.
keyTerminology.importance: Exit status is what &&, ||, and monitoring rely on to know if a step worked, and /dev/null is the standard way to silence output you do not want to see or keep.

importantConcepts.concept: stdout and stderr are two different channels
importantConcepts.explanation: What it is: normal results go to standard output (fd 1) while errors and warnings go to standard error (fd 2), even though by default both land on your screen. Why it matters: if you redirect only stdout to a file (e.g. results.txt), error messages still appear on screen and never pollute your data - and you can capture or discard errors separately. How it works: > and | act on stdout only; you must say 2> to touch stderr, and 2>&1 to merge them. Pitfall: writing 'command > out.txt' and expecting the error text to be in out.txt - it will not be, because errors travel on channel 2, not 1.

importantConcepts.concept: Pipes stream data; redirection lands it in a file
importantConcepts.explanation: What it is: a pipe (|) hands data from one running command to another in memory, while redirection (>, >>) writes data to a file on disk. Why it matters: pipes let stages run together on data that may be far too big to fit in memory or a file, whereas redirection is how you persist a result once the pipeline is done. How it works: the shell wires stdout-to-stdin for pipes and stdout-to-file for redirection, before the commands run. Pitfall: using '>' in the middle of what you meant to be a pipe (e.g. 'grep x file > sort' creates a file called 'sort'!) instead of '|' - a very common beginner mix-up.

What it is: chaining operators do not look at a command's text output at all - they look at its exit code, the success/failure number it returns. Why it matters: this is what makes 'download && process' safe - process only runs if download reported success (exit 0), so you never process a file that failed to arrive. How it works: after each command the shell checks the code; && continues on 0, || continues on non-zero. Pitfall: assuming a command 'worked' because it printed something - a command can print output and still exit non-zero, so trust the exit code, not the text.

variationsAndTypes: **Pipe forms:** a plain pipe '|' passes only stdout to the next command; '|&' (in bash) or '2>&1 |' passes both stdout and stderr into the next command, useful when you want to filter error messages too.
**Output redirection:** '>' overwrites the target file (destroying old contents), while '>>' appends to the end - the difference between replacing a dataset and adding to a running daily log.

**Input redirection and here-strings:** '< file' feeds a file into a command's stdin; a here-string ('command <<< "text"') feeds a short literal string, and a here-document (<<EOF ... EOF) feeds a multi-line block.
**Error redirection:** '2> errors.log' captures only errors, '2>/dev/null' discards them, '2>&1' merges errors into wherever stdout goes, and '&>' (bash) sends both streams to one file at once.
**Chaining operators:** ';' runs commands in sequence no matter what; '&&' runs the next only on success; '||' runs the next only on failure; and they combine, as in 'cmd && echo OK || echo FAILED'.
advantages: **Composability:** small single-purpose tools (grep, sort, uniq, wc, cut) snap together with pipes into powerful custom pipelines you build in seconds.
**Memory efficiency:** piped commands stream data record by record, so you can process files far larger than your available memory without ever loading them whole.
**No temporary files:** pipes pass data directly between commands, keeping your workspace clean and avoiding slow disk writes between stages.
**Reliable control flow:** && and || let scripts make correct decisions based on real success or failure, and separating stderr keeps errors out of your results.
disadvantages: **Hidden failures in pipelines:** by default a pipeline's exit status is only that of the last command, so an earlier stage can fail unnoticed unless you set 'pipefail'.
**Easy destructive mistakes:** a stray '>' overwrites a file instantly with no warning or undo, so a typo can wipe out data.
**Order and precedence confusion:** the position of '2>&1' relative to '>' matters, and beginners often merge streams in the wrong order and lose their errors.
**Readability limits:** very long pipelines with many stages can become hard to read and debug, at which point a small script is clearer than a one-liner.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use pipes and redirection to quickly search, filter, transform, and summarize text and CSV data; to save or append results to files; to silence or capture errors; and use && / || to sequence steps like download-then-process safely, especially for one-off investigations and simple automation.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Reach for a real script or a proper data tool when the logic grows complex (many branches, structured parsing of JSON or nested formats), when you need robust error handling and testing, or when a pipeline would become so long it is harder to read than a few clear lines of code.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Imagine a factory assembly line for sorting mail. Each worker does one small job: one pulls out only the letters marked 'URGENT' (grep), the next stacks them by address (sort), the next bundles duplicates and writes the count on each bundle (uniq -c), and the last arranges bundles biggest-first (sort -nr). The conveyor belt between workers is the pipe - each worker's out-tray flows straight to the next worker's in-tray. At the end, the finished bundles are dropped into a labelled box (redirection to a file), while any 'damaged item' notices are dropped into a separate complaints bin (standard error) that you can read, file, or ignore. And a supervisor's checklist - 'unload the truck, and only if that succeeds, start sorting' - is your && chaining.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The pipe | and the redirect > do the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are different. A pipe (|) sends output to another command as its input; a redirect (>) sends output into a file on disk. Writing 'grep x file > sort' does not pipe into sort - it creates a file literally named 'sort'. Use | to connect commands and > to write to files.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Redirecting output with > also captures error messages.
commonMisconceptions.reality: By default > only redirects standard output (fd 1). Error messages travel on standard error (fd 2) and will still appear on screen. To capture them too you must add 2> or 2>&1 (or use &>), because they are a separate channel.

commonMisconceptions.myth: In 'cmd > file 2>&1' you can put 2>&1 before the > and get the same result.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Order matters. 2>&1 means 'make stderr go wherever stdout currently goes'. If you write '2>&1 > file', stderr is pointed at the screen (stdout's original place) and then stdout is moved to the file - so errors still hit the screen. The correct order is '> file 2>&1'.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Pipelines stream data one chunk at a time with automatic back-pressure, so the same command works on a tiny sample or a multi-gigabyte log, and it drops unchanged into scripts that loop over thousands of files.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Using '&&' between steps ensures a stage runs only after the previous one truly succeeded, and setting 'set -o pipefail' in scripts makes a whole pipeline fail if any stage fails, preventing silent partial results.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Because each command reports an exit code, scripts can detect a failed download or empty file and stop, retry, or alert instead of feeding bad data downstream; '||' provides a clear fallback path.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Redirecting stdout to result files and stderr to a dated error log (2>> errors_$(date +%F).log) creates an audit trail of what each run produced and what went wrong, which is the basis of pipeline monitoring.
productionConsiderations.security: Be careful redirecting to files with '>' as it silently overwrites; use 'set -o noclobber' to prevent accidental overwrites, and never pipe untrusted input into commands that could execute it.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Filtering and summarizing large files with lightweight streaming tools avoids loading them into memory-heavy applications or clusters, cutting both compute cost and time for simple questions.
productionConsiderations.performance: Prefer letting one tool do work rather than many trivial stages, place the most selective filter (like grep) early to shrink the stream fast, and avoid needless intermediate files by piping directly.

codeExamples.title: Count the most common error types in a log with a pipeline
codeExamples.overview: The classic data-engineering one-liner: search a log for errors, then sort, count, and rank them - a whole mini report built from four small tools connected by pipes.
codeExamples.code:
# Find all lines containing ERROR, then rank error lines by how often they occur
grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

# Step it up: read each stage's job
# grep ERROR app.log   -> keep only lines with the word ERROR
# sort                 -> put identical lines next to each other
# uniq -c              -> collapse duplicates and prefix each with a count
# sort -nr             -> sort numerically, highest count first
# head                 -> show only the top 10 lines

# Save the ranked summary to a file instead of the screen
grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr > error_summary.txt
codeExamples.breakdown: 'grep ERROR app.log' reads the file and emits only matching lines to stdout. The first pipe sends them to 'sort', which groups identical lines. 'uniq -c' needs its input sorted, then collapses each group into one line with a leading count. 'sort -nr' sorts numerically (-n) in reverse (-r) so the biggest counts come first. 'head' trims to the top 10. The final version replaces 'head' with '> error_summary.txt', which writes the whole ranked list into a file (overwriting it) rather than printing it.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
142 ERROR Timeout connecting to database
     87 ERROR Null value in required field user_id
     31 ERROR Failed to parse row: malformed CSV
     12 ERROR Disk quota exceeded
      4 ERROR Unknown internal error
codeExamples.commonIssues: If you forget the first 'sort', 'uniq -c' only removes adjacent duplicates and gives wrong counts. Writing '> sort' by mistake instead of '| sort' creates a file named 'sort'. grep is case-sensitive, so 'error' would miss 'ERROR' - add -i to ignore case.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Put the most selective filter (grep) first so later stages handle far less data. Use 'grep -c ERROR app.log' if you only need the total count, which is much faster than a full pipeline.

codeExamples.title: Redirection and chaining: extract a column, save it, silence noise, and gate a step
codeExamples.overview: A tour of the redirection and chaining operators on realistic CSV and download tasks, showing >, >>, <, 2>/dev/null, and &&.
codeExamples.code:
# Extract the 3rd column (email) from a comma-separated file and save it (overwrite)
cut -d',' -f3 users.csv > emails.txt

# Append today's row count to a running daily log (do NOT overwrite)
wc -l < users.csv >> daily_counts.log

# Search a folder but throw away the noisy 'Permission denied' errors
grep -r "api_key" /etc 2>/dev/null

# Download a file, and ONLY if that succeeds, process it; otherwise report failure
curl -sf https://data.example.com/sales.csv -o sales.csv \
  && cut -d',' -f1,4 sales.csv > sales_trimmed.csv \
  || echo "Download failed - skipping processing"
codeExamples.breakdown: 'cut -d',' -f3' splits each line on commas (-d) and keeps field 3 (-f3); '> emails.txt' overwrites that file with the result. 'wc -l < users.csv' reads the file via input redirection and prints its line count, and '>> daily_counts.log' appends that number to a log without erasing history. '2>/dev/null' sends standard error (channel 2) into the discard device so 'Permission denied' warnings vanish while real matches still print. The last block uses '&&' so 'cut' runs only if 'curl' succeeded (exit 0), and '||' so the echo runs only if something before it failed - a safe download-then-process gate.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ cat emails.txt
alice@example.com
bob@example.com
carol@example.com

$ cat daily_counts.log
1043
1058

$ grep -r "api_key" /etc 2>/dev/null
/etc/myapp/config.ini:api_key=REDACTED
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using '>' when you meant '>>' silently wipes your daily log. Omitting quotes/backslashes on the multi-line command breaks the chaining. If curl lacks '-f', it exits 0 even on a 404 and the '&&' step runs on a bad file - '-f' makes curl fail on HTTP errors.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use '2>>errors.log' instead of discarding errors when you might need to investigate later. Group commands with { ...; } or use 'set -o pipefail' in scripts so a mid-pipeline failure is not hidden.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: The analytics team reports that the nightly orders pipeline 'seems flaky'. A data engineer must download today's raw orders file, confirm it arrived intact, extract just the order status column, and produce a ranked summary of how many orders ended in each status (completed, failed, pending) - all from the command line, saving the summary and logging any errors.
endToEndExample.inputData: A remote CSV at https://data.example.com/orders_2026_07_02.csv with a header row and columns order_id,customer_id,amount,status,created_at, roughly 500,000 rows.
endToEndExample.architecture: curl (download over HTTPS) -> && gate on success -> tail (drop header) -> cut (extract status column) -> sort -> uniq -c -> sort -nr (rank statuses) -> redirection > to status_summary.txt, with stderr redirected to a dated error log
processingSteps: 1. Download the file with 'curl -sf ... -o orders.csv'; the -f flag makes curl exit non-zero on any HTTP error so a missing file is caught.
2. Use '&&' so the next steps run only if the download truly succeeded; a trailing '|| echo' branch logs a clear failure message otherwise.
3. Strip the header row with 'tail -n +2 orders.csv' so it is not counted as data, and pipe the result onward.

4. Pipe into 'cut -d',' -f4' to keep only the status column, then 'sort | uniq -c | sort -nr' to count and rank each status, redirecting the final output to status_summary.txt and any errors to a dated log with 2>>.
endToEndExample.output: A small file status_summary.txt containing each order status with its count, ordered from most to least frequent, plus a possibly-empty errors_2026-07-02.log capturing anything that went wrong.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The engineer checks that status_summary.txt is non-empty and that the counts sum to about 500,000 (a quick sanity check with 'wc -l orders.csv'), and inspects the dated error log to confirm it is empty.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If curl fails (network down or 404), '&&' stops the pipeline and the '||' branch writes 'download failed' so no stale file is processed; any per-row read errors are captured to the dated error log via 2>> rather than being lost among results.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A trustworthy one-line-per-status summary showing, for example, 412,003 completed, 61,847 pending, and 26,150 failed orders - produced, saved, and logged entirely with pipes, redirection, and chaining, ready to paste into the team's channel.

industryUseCases.company: Site reliability / platform teams (e.g. any Linux-server operation)
industryUseCases.problem: Production log files grow to gigabytes and engineers must quickly find and rank the errors causing an incident.
industryUseCases.solution: Pipelines like 'grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr' surface the top error types in seconds, and results are redirected to a file for the incident report.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fast root-cause triage during outages without loading logs into any tool, and a saved, shareable summary of what went wrong.

industryUseCases.company: Data ingestion / ETL teams (e.g. teams landing daily CSV feeds)
industryUseCases.problem: Daily files must be downloaded and only processed if they arrive complete, with a running record of row counts kept over time.
industryUseCases.solution: Scripts use 'curl -f ... && process ...' to gate processing on a successful download and '>>' to append each day's row count to a running log for freshness checks.
industryUseCases.benefits: No processing of failed or partial downloads, and an easy historical trail to spot days when data volumes look abnormal.

industryUseCases.company: Analytics engineers doing quick data profiling (e.g. dbt / warehouse teams)
industryUseCases.problem: Before loading a raw file they need to peek at its columns and value distributions without a full ingestion.
industryUseCases.solution: Commands such as 'cut -d',' -f4 file.csv | sort | uniq -c' profile a column's values directly on the file, and '2>/dev/null' silences unrelated noise.
industryUseCases.benefits: Instant, cheap data profiling that catches malformed or unexpected values before they reach the warehouse.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Pipelines stream input so memory stays roughly constant regardless of file size, and back-pressure between stages prevents any one command from overwhelming the others; the same command is embedded in scripts that iterate over thousands of files or run per-server.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Chaining with '&&' guards each dependent step behind the success of the last, '||' provides fallbacks, and 'set -o pipefail' promotes any mid-pipeline failure to a whole-pipeline failure so downstream steps do not consume bad data.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Because these are just shell features available on every Linux host reached over SSH, the same diagnostic and processing pipelines can be run on any node at any time, and automated command-driven health checks run continuously.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Recovery runbooks are written as command sequences using chaining, so restoring or re-running a data step is an exact, repeatable operation; redirection captures each run's output for later verification.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Place the most selective filter early to shrink the stream, prefer a single capable tool over many trivial stages, avoid unnecessary intermediate files by piping directly, and reach for tools like awk when a pipeline of many small commands becomes the bottleneck.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Answering 'how many failures today?' with a grep-and-count pipeline on a cheap server avoids spinning up query engines or clusters, saving compute spend and engineer time for routine questions.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Use 'set -o noclobber' to stop '>' from silently overwriting important files, redirect secrets away from logs, and never pipe untrusted content into an interpreter; discard sensitive stderr with 2>/dev/null only when you are sure you will not need it.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Redirect stdout to result files and stderr to dated logs (2>> errors_$(date +%F).log) so every run leaves an auditable trail of results and errors that monitoring can scrape and alert on.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Quick pipelines act as first-line quality gates: 'wc -l' checks row counts, 'cut ... | sort | uniq -c' checks a column's value distribution, and an empty grep result can flag missing expected records before heavy processing runs.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Scripts capture each stage's output and exit code, append failures to a log with '>>', and use '|| alert-command' so that a non-zero exit anywhere in the flow triggers a notification, turning the pipeline into an early-warning system.

recommendedPractices: **Use | to connect commands and > to write files** - never confuse them; remember 'grep x file > sort' creates a file named sort instead of piping.
**Prefer >> for logs and > only when you truly mean to replace a file**, so you never accidentally erase a running record.
**Redirect errors deliberately** with 2> to a log or 2>/dev/null to discard, and use 2>&1 (in the correct position, after >) when you need both streams together.
**Gate dependent steps with &&** so processing runs only after a successful download or check, and add '|| echo/alert' for a clear failure path.
engineeringStandards: In scripts, set 'set -o pipefail' so a failure in any pipeline stage is not hidden by a successful final stage.
Ensure 'uniq' input is sorted first, since uniq only collapses adjacent duplicate lines.
Always quote the delimiter and arguments (e.g. cut -d',' -f3) and check exit codes rather than assuming a command succeeded.
designRecommendations: Build pipelines incrementally: add one stage at a time and inspect the output before piping it onward.
Put the most selective filter (grep) first to reduce how much data later stages process.
When a one-liner grows past a few stages or needs branching, move it into a small documented script instead.
namingConventions: Give redirected output files clear, descriptive names (error_summary.txt, sales_trimmed.csv) rather than out.txt or temp.
Include dates in appended log names (errors_2026-07-02.log or errors_$(date +%F).log) so runs are distinguishable.
Refer to streams precisely by name and number - stdout (1), stderr (2), stdin (0) - so instructions and error handling are unambiguous.
documentationStandards: Add a comment above non-trivial pipelines explaining what each stage does, since they are terse and easy to misread later.
Note any assumptions, such as 'input must be sorted' or 'curl -f is required so a 404 fails the chain'.
Record which shell (bash vs sh) a script targets, because features like &> and |& are bash-specific.
testingStrategies: Test destructive redirection on a copy first, and use 'set -o noclobber' while experimenting so '>' cannot overwrite a real file.
Run each stage of a pipeline alone (and pipe into 'head') on a small sample to confirm its output before chaining everything.
Deliberately trigger the failure branch (e.g. a bad URL) to confirm '&&' and '||' behave as intended before relying on them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running 'uniq -c' without sorting the input first and getting inflated or wrong counts.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Beginners assume uniq counts all identical lines anywhere in the file, but it only collapses lines that are adjacent to each other.
commonMistakes.impact: The summary shows the same value multiple times with partial counts, silently producing an incorrect report.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always pipe through 'sort' before 'uniq -c' (grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c) so identical lines are grouped together first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using '>' to write output when you meant to append, wiping out an existing file.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: '>' and '>>' look almost identical and the overwrite happens instantly with no confirmation or undo.
commonMistakes.impact: A running log or a previous result is destroyed the moment the command runs, and there is no recovery.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use '>>' whenever you want to add to a file, reserve '>' for deliberate replacement, and enable 'set -o noclobber' to be warned before overwriting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting 'command > file' to also capture error messages in the file.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: On screen stdout and stderr are mixed together, so it is easy to forget they are separate channels (1 and 2).
commonMistakes.impact: Error messages are missed entirely - either lost from the saved output or unexpectedly cluttering the screen - making failures hard to diagnose.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Redirect errors explicitly: '2> errors.log' to capture them separately, '2>&1' after '> file' to merge them into the file, or '2>/dev/null' to discard them on purpose.

comparisonSection.feature: Connecting output to the next step
comparisonSection.explanation: A pipe streams one command's output directly into another command's input, in memory, with both running at once - ideal for chaining filters like grep, sort, and uniq. A redirect writes output to a file on disk, which is how you persist a final result or feed it to a later, separate command. They solve different problems: use | to keep data moving through a pipeline, and > (or >>) to land the finished data somewhere. Confusing them ('> command') accidentally creates a file named after the command.

comparisonSection.feature: Overwrite versus append when writing to a file
comparisonSection.explanation: '>' opens the target file, discards any existing contents, and writes fresh output - perfect for a summary you want to regenerate each run. '>>' opens the file in append mode and adds to the end, preserving history - exactly what you want for a daily log or a running count. The risk is asymmetric: using '>>' where you meant '>' just leaves extra old data, but using '>' where you meant '>>' permanently destroys the previous contents, so append is the safer default when in doubt.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a pipe (|) and output redirection (>)?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A pipe (|) connects one command's standard output to the next command's standard input so data flows between running programs. Output redirection (>) sends a command's standard output into a file on disk (overwriting it), while >> appends to the file. In short, | passes data to a command, > passes data to a file.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to confirm you understand that pipes are command-to-command and redirects are command-to-file. A great answer notes that mixing them up (e.g. '> sort' instead of '| sort') creates a file rather than piping.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are stdin, stdout, and stderr, and what are their file descriptor numbers?
beginnerQuestions.answer: They are the three standard streams every program gets: standard input (stdin, fd 0) is where it reads input, standard output (stdout, fd 1) is where it writes normal results, and standard error (stderr, fd 2) is where it writes error and diagnostic messages. Both stdout and stderr go to the screen by default but are separate channels.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This checks the foundation for all redirection. Mentioning the numbers 0, 1, 2 and that errors are separate from results shows you can reason about 2>, 2>&1, and /dev/null.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you count how many times each distinct value appears in a column of a CSV, and why is sort needed?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Extract the column and pipe it through sort then uniq -c: 'cut -d',' -f4 file.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr'. sort is needed because uniq only collapses and counts lines that are adjacent, so the input must be sorted first for the counts to be correct; the final 'sort -nr' ranks the results by count.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This tests real pipeline-building and the classic gotcha that uniq requires sorted input. Adding 'sort -nr' at the end shows you know how to rank the summary.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between '&&', '||', and ';' when chaining commands?
intermediateQuestions.answer: ';' runs the commands in sequence regardless of whether each succeeds. '&&' runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded (exit code 0). '||' runs the next command only if the previous one failed (non-zero exit code). They rely on exit status, not on the text output.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A strong answer ties the operators to exit codes and gives a use case, e.g. 'download && process || alert', proving understanding of conditional flow control.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the difference between 'cmd > file 2>&1' and 'cmd 2>&1 > file'.
advancedQuestions.answer: 'cmd > file 2>&1' first points stdout at the file, then makes stderr go wherever stdout now points - so both end up in the file. 'cmd 2>&1 > file' first makes stderr copy stdout's current target (the terminal), then moves stdout to the file - so stderr still goes to the terminal and only stdout lands in the file. Order matters because 2>&1 captures stdout's destination at that moment.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This separates candidates who truly understand that redirections are applied left to right and that 2>&1 duplicates the current target of fd 1, a very common source of bugs.

advancedQuestions.question: By default, what is a pipeline's exit status, and how do you make it fail if any stage fails?
advancedQuestions.answer: By default a pipeline's exit status is the exit status of its last command only, so an earlier stage can fail while the pipeline still reports success. To make the pipeline fail if any stage fails, set 'set -o pipefail' (in bash), which makes the pipeline return the status of the last command that exited non-zero.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Shows awareness of a real production pitfall - silent mid-pipeline failures - and knowledge of pipefail as the standard remedy in robust scripts.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You run 'grep WARN service.log > warnings.txt' but warnings.txt is empty even though warnings clearly print on your screen. What is going on?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Output redirected with > captures only stdout (fd 1). If what I see on screen is actually being written to standard error (fd 2) by the program, then > will not capture it, which explains an empty file while text still appears on screen. I should confirm by checking whether the tool writes to stderr, and then redirect the correct stream.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: The messages are being written to standard error, not standard output, so '> warnings.txt' (which only redirects stdout) leaves the file empty. Capture stderr instead - e.g. 'grep WARN service.log 2> warnings.txt' - or merge both with 'grep WARN service.log > warnings.txt 2>&1' if you want everything in one file.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a nightly command-line job that downloads a daily CSV, processes it only if the download succeeds, keeps a running history of row counts, and alerts on failure.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use 'curl -sf URL -o data.csv' so an HTTP error fails the command, then '&&' to run the processing pipeline (strip header with tail, extract and summarize columns with cut/sort/uniq, redirecting the result to a dated file). Append the row count to a running log with 'wc -l < data.csv >> daily_counts.log', capture errors with '2>> errors_$(date +%F).log', and add '|| send-alert' so any failure notifies the team. Wrap it in a script with 'set -o pipefail' and schedule it.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: A command pipeline is fast to build and cheap to run but can hide mid-pipeline failures without pipefail and becomes hard to maintain if logic grows; a full data tool is more robust but heavier. Overwriting vs appending must be chosen deliberately to protect history.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Parameterize the date and URL, loop the script over multiple feeds or servers, centralize the dated logs for monitoring, and if a single feed grows too large or the logic branches heavily, promote the one-liner to a maintained script or a proper ingestion tool.

followUpQuestions: How would you discard a command's error messages while still seeing its normal output?
Why does 'uniq' require its input to be sorted, and what happens if it is not?
What does /dev/null do, and when would you redirect to it?
How can you feed the contents of a file into a command's standard input without using cat?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Pipes (|) feed one command's output into the next, redirection (>, >>, <, 2>, &>) moves streams to and from files, and chaining (;, &&, ||) sequences commands by success or failure - the tools for building command-line data pipelines.
keyConcepts: Three streams: stdin (0) in, stdout (1) normal output, stderr (2) errors - stdout and stderr are separate channels.
Pipe | connects command-to-command; redirect > / >> connects command-to-file (overwrite / append).
2> redirects errors, 2>&1 merges errors into stdout (order matters - put it after >), /dev/null discards.
; runs always, && runs next only on success (exit 0), || runs next only on failure (non-zero).
uniq -c needs sorted input; a pipeline's exit status is its last command unless you set -o pipefail.
commands: grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr   # rank error types by frequency
cut -d',' -f3 users.csv > emails.txt             # extract column 3, overwrite file
wc -l < users.csv >> daily_counts.log            # append this file's line count to a log
grep -r api_key /etc 2>/dev/null                 # search, discarding permission errors
command > out.txt 2>&1                           # send both stdout and stderr to one file
download.sh && process.sh || echo FAILED         # process only if download succeeds, else report
sort data.txt | uniq -c | sort -nr | head        # top values by count
interviewPoints: Pipe (command-to-command) vs redirect (command-to-file), and the '> sort' pitfall.
stdin/stdout/stderr are fds 0/1/2; > only captures stdout, use 2> for errors.
Order matters: '> file 2>&1' captures both, '2>&1 > file' does not.
&& / || / ; are driven by exit codes (0 = success), not by text output.
uniq -c needs sorted input; use set -o pipefail so mid-pipeline failures are not hidden.
quickNotes: Build pipelines one stage at a time and pipe into 'head' to preview safely.
Prefer >> for logs; > overwrites instantly with no undo (set -o noclobber to guard).
2>/dev/null silences errors; 2>>errors.log keeps them for later.
curl -f makes a 404 fail the command so && will not process a bad file.
Put the most selective filter (grep) first to shrink the data early.

keyTakeaways: Every command has three text streams - stdin (0) for input, stdout (1) for normal results, and stderr (2) for errors - and understanding that results and errors travel on separate channels is the key to controlling them.
A pipe (|) streams one command's output into the next so small tools like grep, sort, uniq, wc, and cut combine into powerful one-line data pipelines without any temporary files.

Redirection moves streams to and from files: > overwrites, >> appends, < reads input, 2> handles errors, 2>&1 merges them (order matters), and 2>/dev/null discards - so you can save results and route errors deliberately.

Chaining operators run on exit codes: ; always runs the next command, && runs it only on success, and || runs it only on failure, which makes safe patterns like 'download && process || alert' possible.
Watch the classic pitfalls - sort before uniq -c, use >> instead of > for logs, remember > does not capture errors, and set -o pipefail so a failing stage in a pipeline is never silently ignored.
